findings.title: "Name for a secret" exemption is a substring check, letting real passphrases bypass the scanner
findings.detail: onlyNames() decides a quoted value is "just a name" if it whole-matches a camelCase/dash-joined word pattern and lower.contains(any of ["secret","token","password","passwd","key","client","vault","entry","access","name","id"]). This is a bare substring test over the whole value, not a check that the value actually equals/names the assigned key, and several of the trigger words ("id", "name", "key", "access") are extremely common English substrings. As a result a genuine secret value that happens to be a readable, digit-free phrase slips through undetected, directly contradicting the change's own promise that "passphrases ... still count". Concrete example: `password = "temporary-access-code"` matches the "password or secret" rule's regex (value is 22 chars, no quotes/spaces), onlyNames() whole-matches the dash-word regex and lower.contains("access") is true, so breaks() returns false and Publish.matches() reports no finding at all — a real secret is now silently allowed to be pushed. The same happens for any value containing "id" (e.g. "valid-user-identity"), "name" ("renamed-access-granted"), "key", "client", "vault" or "entry" as a substring, regardless of whether the value actually names the field it's assigned to.
